title: Remote state preparation from quantum-secure one-way functions
formal:
Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against quantum polynomial-time inversion with quantum advice imply the existence of a protocol for parallel remote preparation of BB84 states with the inverse-polynomial rigidity guarantee defined below? In symbols, decide
\[
\bigl(\exists F\;\operatorname{QOWF}(F)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\exists\Pi\;\operatorname{RSP}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\Pi)\bigr).
\]
The protocol has one classical client and one quantum server, uses only classical communication, and has no trusted setup or initially shared resource. The client chooses a basis string \(\theta\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), and upon acceptance obtains a string \(v\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). For an honest server, its designated output register contains the corresponding BB84 product state
\[
|\psi_{v,\theta}\rangle=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}H^{\theta_{i}}|v_{i}\rangle,
\qquad H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
with uniformly random \(v\), up to negligible correctness error. Against any efficient malicious server, the accepted joint output must satisfy the computational rigidity condition below, up to an efficient isometry on the server’s space and an auxiliary state independent of \(v,\theta\). A unary accuracy parameter \(t\) permits soundness error \(1/t\) plus a negligible term, with resources polynomial in the security parameter \(\lambda\), \(n\), and \(t\).

This is a documented selection of the original paper’s own inverse-polynomial, isometry-based guarantee from its broader question about an RSP-like protocol. The target is an implication between existence statements, not a prescribed black-box reduction or a requirement for negligible simulation error.
why: Remote preparation asks how a classical participant can cause an untrusted quantum device to hold useful hidden quantum states using only classical messages. Identifying whether ordinary one-way-function hardness suffices would clarify which cryptographic resources are essential for this form of classical control, beyond the more structured assumptions in known constructions.
status_note: The source explicitly poses OWF-only RSP in ICALP 2023, but leaves RSP-like and sufficiently-strong-parameters variants open. This card transparently selects its own parallel BB84 inverse-polynomial rigidity guarantee, using the full-version quantum-advice and accepted-mass conventions. Primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found later constructions under structured trapdoor assumptions and oracle impossibility results with additional restrictions, but no resolution of this exact standard-model implication. Negligible simulation soundness is a separate stronger target. Current status remains source_open with bounded-review limits.

progress.text: Gheorghiu, Metger and Poremba construct parallel BB84 remote state preparation from quantum-advice-secure Learning With Errors. The security conclusion is computational rigidity up to an efficient isometry, with adjustable inverse-polynomial error on the accepted subnormalized state; the concluding question asks about one-way functions and separately discusses negligible soundness.

Zhang distinguishes rigidity-based and simulation-based formulations of remote state preparation with verifiability and develops constructions from weak noisy trapdoor claw-free functions, including group-action instantiations. These hypotheses impose more structure than an arbitrary one-way function.

Bartusek and Khurana study oblivious state preparation, which hides a basis choice while requiring correctness for an honest receiver. Their constructions use trapdoor claw-free functions, and their consequences include classical-communication oblivious transfer; the stated quantum-random-oracle impossibility concerns perfectly correct OSP. The paper explicitly cautions that OSP has no generic simulation guarantee.

Bartusek, Liu and Malavolta obtain new classical verification applications from oblivious state preparation and collapsing hash functions. Their assumptions retain OSP, available from plain trapdoor claw-free functions, rather than deriving it from arbitrary quantum-secure one-way functions.

Li, Li, Li and Liu’s preprint gives a query-bounded attack on perfectly complete, arbitrarily many-round quantum key agreement with classical communication in the quantum random-oracle model. Its perfect-completeness and oracle restrictions do not establish nonexistence of the imperfectly correct standard-model protocol asked for here.

Kitagawa, Nishimaki, Villányi and Yamakawa’s preprint extends oracle attacks to imperfect completeness in two-message protocols with classical-query first-stage key generation, and in multi-round protocols whose prefix uses only classical oracle queries. The arbitrary-round remote-preparation target here does not impose those restrictions.

importance.reason: A broad cryptographic foundations question about whether the weakest standard classical computational primitive can support classical control of an untrusted quantum system. Parallel hidden-state preparation supports several distinct quantum cryptographic applications, and the assumption gap connects to the limits of classical-communication secure computation. The precise retained target is the source’s inverse-polynomial rigidity form, not an automatically strengthened composable primitive; score 87 is a new individual editorial assessment replacing an unassessed 50.

sentences: Remote state preparation lets a classical client use classical messages to leave a quantum server holding states whose descriptions are known to the client.
This card asks whether quantum-advice-secure classical one-way functions suffice for the source’s parallel BB84 protocol guarantee.

Its accepted output must resemble independent uniformly valued BB84 states up to an efficient server-side isometry, with tunable inverse-polynomial computational error and advice independent of the hidden basis.
Known constructions use more structured trapdoor assumptions, while later papers distinguish this rigidity guarantee from basis hiding and composable simulation.
The selected model is an explicit editorial interpretation of the broad source question, and checked oracle barriers do not refute its full standard-model existence implication.

definitions:
A function \(\nu:\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if, for every integer \(c\ge1\), there is \(\lambda_{0}\) such that \(\nu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\) for every \(\lambda\ge\lambda_{0}\). All negligible errors below are with respect to \(\lambda\).

Classical computation uses ordinary multitape Turing machines over a fixed finite alphabet, with unary security and public size parameters and binary strings as data. One transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Classical randomness consists of independent fair bits, each charged as a step. A uniform quantum computation has a classical polynomial-time machine that, on the unary public parameters, prints its polynomial-size circuit description. Circuits use the finite gate set consisting of Hadamard \(H\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4})\), controlled-NOT, computational-basis measurements, and classical Boolean control; ancillas start in \(|0\rangle\). Controlled-NOT maps \(|a,b\rangle\) to \(|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\), and \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. Gates and wire indices have finite binary descriptions. Adaptive operations are controlled by recorded classical measurement results. Circuit generation, classical steps, quantum gates, measurements, output writing and communication are all charged. An interactive quantum strategy is a uniform sequence of these operations between messages, with total operations and qubits bounded by a fixed polynomial in the public input length on every branch. An inverse unitary can use the same gate set since \(T^{-1}=T^{7}\). The choice of this particular universal finite gate set is a modeling convention.

For adversarial computation and the auxiliary efficient procedures in the rigidity condition, allow quantum advice: a polynomial number of extra qubits in an arbitrary density operator depending on the public parameters but independent of the private challenge, client coins and hidden input. The advice need not be efficiently preparable. An advice family is fixed together with the algorithm before an experiment is sampled. Different public parameter tuples may have different advice, and all such families are quantified over. This uses the original full paper’s explicit advice convention, including in the hardness assumption. Honest protocol algorithms use no advice. An isometry is a linear map \(J\) satisfying \(J^{\dagger}J=I\); efficient implementation means a circuit of the preceding kind acting unitarily on the input with additional pure ancillas, retaining all output qubits. Pure quantum advice independent of the private input is permitted for such an auxiliary isometry. Mixed advice may be purified by enlarging the ancillary space. An efficiently preparable auxiliary state means the output of an efficient procedure under this same advice convention, not that its advice can itself be generated from a classical description.

The one-way-function premise \(\operatorname{QOWF}(F)\) has the following meaning. There are an output-length function \(\ell(\lambda)\ge1\), bounded by a fixed polynomial, and a single deterministic polynomial-time classical algorithm evaluating
\(F_{\lambda}:\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(\lambda)}\)
on input \((1^{\lambda},x)\). For every uniform quantum polynomial-time inverter \(I\), with any polynomial-size quantum-advice family \((\eta_{\lambda})\), there is a negligible \(\nu_{I,\eta}\) such that
\[
\Pr_{x\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{\lambda}}\!\left[
z\in\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\ \land\ F_{\lambda}(z)=F_{\lambda}(x)
\ :\ z\leftarrow I(1^{\lambda},F_{\lambda}(x);\eta_{\lambda})
\right]\le\nu_{I,\eta}(\lambda).
\]
The probability includes the inverter’s measurements and random bits. Any preimage is a successful inversion; injectivity, a trapdoor, length preservation and hardness of recovering the particular sampled preimage are not required. The evaluator’s public program is available to the inverter, which may implement it coherently. There is no random oracle in this assumption.

The remote-state-preparation protocol \(\Pi=(A,B_{\mathrm{hon}})\) consists of a single probabilistic classical client algorithm \(A\) and a single uniform quantum honest-server algorithm \(B_{\mathrm{hon}}\). Their public inputs are \((1^{\lambda},1^{n},1^{t})\), with \(\lambda,n,t\ge1\), and only the client receives \(\theta\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). Inputs are encoded as the unary blocks separated by the fixed symbol \(\#\), followed on the client’s input tape by the binary basis string. The number of rounds, total communicated bits, client runtime, honest-server operations and honest-server qubits are bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(\lambda+n+t\). Communication is a reliable classical channel; any message produced by a quantum party is measured in the computational basis before delivery. Private classical coins are independent, and the honest parties initially share no secret, randomness or entanglement. There are no oracles, quantum messages, auxiliary devices, additional servers or trusted setup. The protocol specifies polynomial message-length and round limits, with a malformed or overlong message, missing prescribed response, or limit violation causing the client to abort. The client finally outputs an accept/reject flag and, when accepting, the classical string \(v\). The server may retain its entire transcript and private quantum workspace.

For fixed \(\lambda,n,t,\theta\), define the ideal classical–quantum state on registers \(WQ\) by
\[
\Omega^{\theta}_{WQ}
=2^{-n}\sum_{v\in\{0,1\}^{n}}|v\rangle\langle v|_{W}
\otimes|\psi_{v,\theta}\rangle\langle\psi_{v,\theta}|_{Q}.
\]
Here \(W\) is a classical register represented in its computational basis, and \(Q\) contains \(n\) qubits. A density operator is a positive semidefinite operator of trace one; a subnormalized state has trace at most one. The trace norm is \(\|X\|_{1}=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^{\dagger}X}\), and trace distance is \(\tfrac12\|X-Y\|_{1}\).

Completeness and honest correctness mean the following. For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), there is a negligible function \(\mu_{c}\) such that for all \(\lambda\), all \(1\le n,t\le\lambda^{c}\), and every basis string \(\theta\), the honest run accepts with probability at least \(1-\mu_{c}(\lambda)\). Let \(\rho^{\theta,\mathrm{hon}}_{WQ,\mathrm{acc}}\) be its accepted joint output, after tracing out other registers and weighting by the acceptance probability. Require
\[
\tfrac12\bigl\|\rho^{\theta,\mathrm{hon}}_{WQ,\mathrm{acc}}-
\Omega^{\theta}_{WQ}\bigr\|_{1}\le\mu_{c}(\lambda).
\]
Thus no exact correctness or perfect acceptance is imposed, and uniformity of the honest value string is included in the guarantee.

For soundness, let \(B^{*}\) be any quantum polynomial-time interactive server, including a fixed quantum-advice family independent of \(\theta\). Let \(P\) be all its final registers, including classical transcripts, and write
\[
\rho^{\theta}_{WP,\mathrm{acc}}
=\Pr[\mathrm{acc}\mid\theta]\,
\rho^{\theta}_{WP\mid\mathrm{acc}},
\qquad p_{\theta}=\operatorname{Tr}\rho^{\theta}_{WP,\mathrm{acc}}.
\]
The accepted operator is defined as zero when acceptance has probability zero, so conditional normalization is never needed. There must exist a family of efficiently implementable isometries
\(J_{\lambda,n,t}:P\to QB\)
and efficiently preparable normalized states \(\alpha_{\lambda,n,t}\) on the residual register \(B\). Their algorithms, dimensions and polynomial resource bounds may depend on \(B^{*}\) and its fixed advice family, and their values may depend on the public tuple \((\lambda,n,t)\). They must be chosen before the distinguisher, must not depend on \(\theta\) or \(v\), and act only on the server’s systems and independent ancillas. All advice used by these auxiliary procedures is independent of \(\theta,v\) and the sampled protocol randomness.

Define the two subnormalized operators
\[
R^{\theta}=(I_{W}\otimes J_{\lambda,n,t})\rho^{\theta}_{WP,\mathrm{acc}}
(I_{W}\otimes J_{\lambda,n,t})^{\dagger},
\qquad
S^{\theta}=p_{\theta}\,\Omega^{\theta}_{WQ}\otimes\alpha_{\lambda,n,t}.
\]
For every quantum polynomial-time distinguisher \(D\), including its independent polynomial-size quantum advice, and every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), there must be a negligible function \(\nu_{B^{*},D,c}\) such that, simultaneously for every \(\lambda\), every \(1\le n,t\le\lambda^{c}\), and every \(\theta\in\{0,1\}^{n}\),
\[
\left|\Pr[D(R^{\theta})=1]-\Pr[D(S^{\theta})=1]\right|
\le\frac1t+\nu_{B^{*},D,c}(\lambda).
\]
The distinguisher receives the public tuple and \(\theta\), as well as registers \(WQB\), but no additional client workspace, private randomness or secret data. Allowing the fixed basis as a test parameter makes explicit the source’s statement for each basis choice; it is not information sent to the server during the protocol. Its advice is independent of the sampled run. For a subnormalized operator \(X\), the expression \(\Pr[D(X)=1]\) denotes the linear acceptance functional \(\operatorname{Tr}(E_{D}X)\), where \(0\le E_{D}\le I\) is the effect implemented by \(D\), including its fixed advice. This convention applies without dividing by \(\operatorname{Tr}X\).

The soundness quantifier order is: choose the protocol, then quantify over the malicious server and its advice, then choose its common extraction isometry and auxiliary-state procedures, then quantify over distinguishers and polynomial parameter ranges, then choose the negligible errors, and finally quantify over parameters and basis strings. No lower bound on a malicious server’s acceptance probability is required. Only accepted mass is constrained, and its weight \(p_{\theta}\) is retained; no additional claim about the rejected output is imposed. The adjustable accuracy has polynomial cost in \(t\), and security is required when \(n,t\) are polynomially bounded in \(\lambda\). It therefore specifies arbitrarily adjustable inverse-polynomial soundness, not a single polynomial-time protocol with negligible soundness, and not a composable simulation definition.

The selected guarantee follows the roles, output states, efficient-isometry form and quantum-advice convention of the source’s Theorem 4.33 and Corollary 4.35. Packaging accuracy as a unary input and giving explicit uniform parameter-range and gate conventions are editorial precisions. The original question also discusses RSP with sufficiently strong parameters for further cryptographic applications; this card does not identify that stronger possibility with the guarantee selected here.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
(\exists F\;\operatorname{QOWF}(F))
\Rightarrow(\exists\Pi\;\operatorname{RSP}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\Pi))
\]
or its logical negation, for exactly the definitions above.

A positive answer must establish the existence of the client and honest-server algorithms, their uniform polynomial bounds, negligible honest correctness error, and the accepted-state rigidity property with its full malicious-server, advice, isometry, auxiliary-state, distinguisher and parameter quantifiers, using only the stated existence of a quantum-advice-secure classical one-way function. No efficient compiler taking an arbitrary one-way-function description as input, black-box use of that function, or preservation of a supplied security parameter is required beyond the definitions.

A negative answer must prove both
\[
\exists F\;\operatorname{QOWF}(F)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\forall\Pi\;\neg\operatorname{RSP}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\Pi).
\]
The second quantifier ranges over all finite descriptions of protocol pairs in the stated standard model; failure may concern uniform efficiency, completeness, correctness or the entire quantified soundness property. Merely showing that one proposed construction fails, that a black-box reduction is impossible relative to an oracle, or that a stronger perfect-correctness, negligible-error or composable functionality is impossible does not refute this implication. Conversely, a protocol under a stronger cryptographic assumption or for only an honest or classical server does not establish the positive implication. No numerical-answer tolerance replaces any error bound in this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The source explicitly asks whether quantum-secure one-way functions can support an RSP-like protocol and discusses possible impossibility when the parameters are strong enough for further cryptographic applications.

This card selects the source’s parallel BB84 rigidity guarantee with adjustable inverse-polynomial soundness, while making the public parameters, quantum advice and computational conventions explicit.
The original construction uses quantum-hard Learning With Errors, and the source treats negligible soundness as a separate unresolved strengthening.

Later work distinguishes isometry-based rigidity, simulation-based verifiability and oblivious state preparation, so their constructions and consequences cannot be interchanged without matching definitions.
The checked oracle impossibility results have completeness, round or query restrictions and do not constitute a refutation of this standard-model implication.

Source-to-model precision: retain chosen basis theta and random values v, all n-qubit BB84 tensor products, general malicious quantum server, no success-probability promise. Represent accepted output directly as a subnormalized positive operator of trace p_theta; ideal state has the SAME p_theta factor. Use one common extraction isometry and normalized auxiliary state independent of theta,v, with polynomial-size dimensions and advice-aware efficient preparation. Chosen parameter t realizes error 1/t at polynomial cost, equivalent to the adjustable inverse-polynomial regime of source parameters; no exponential precision or negligible soundness with polynomial runtime is demanded. Honest output and acceptance are negligible-error, not exact. All asymptotic errors are uniform on each polynomial range of n,t in lambda, avoiding undefined poly dependencies.

One-way-functions model is classical deterministic uniform evaluation on lambda-bit uniformly sampled inputs, polynomial output length, any-preimage hardness against all QPT inverters with independent polynomial-size quantum advice, negligible success. No injectivity/trapdoor/regularity/homomorphism assumption. The implication compares existence, with no black-box-construction, reduction compiler or seed preservation requirement. The negative Lean theorem must prove existence of a QOWF and failure of every qualifying RSP protocol in this standard model; the cited oracle limitations cannot establish it by themselves.
